item.research_question: How can yield strength be enhanced in metastable austenitic steels without sacrificing ductility, specifically by utilizing dislocation strengthening mechanisms that do not impede the nucleation of new dislocations required for plastic deformation?
item.processing_route: One-step thermal mechanical treatment (TMT) via hot rolling at 450 °C with thickness reductions of 10% and 20%; initial material was solid solution treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 1×10−3 s−1; in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) at 200 kV using a stepwise displacement loading mode.
key_findings: Yield strength increased from 322 ± 18 MPa to 675 ± 15 MPa with 20% thickness reduction.
Uniform elongation increased from 54% ± 3% to 71% ± 2% with 20% thickness reduction.
Dislocation density reached approximately 10^15 m−2 in the sample with 20% reduction.
No grain boundaries or cellular substructures were introduced by the optimized TMT process.
Phase transformation (α-martensite) nucleated at an earlier stage of deformation in TMT samples compared to solid solution treated samples.
Martensite growth terminated at high-angle grain boundaries or twin boundaries due to coherency dependence.
Lamella spacing between intercalated α-martensite and austenite was approximately 500 nm before fracture.
item.mechanism: The success relies on decoupled strengthening and toughening mechanisms where yield strength is controlled by the initial dislocation density (which impedes motion), while ductility is retained because the pre-stored dislocations do not pin phase boundaries but instead promote phase transformation and serve as effective dislocation sources via stress singularities at terraced phase boundaries, allowing new dislocations to be nucleated to carry plastic deformation.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the complexity of the underlying mechanism may require further investigation.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that following the guideline of decoupling strengthening and toughening mechanisms, other methods may be developed to enhance material performance in metal manufacturing.
quotes: yield strength is controlled by initial dislocation density while ductility is retained by the capability to nucleate new dislocations to carry plastic deformation.
hot rolling is an effective way in injecting dislocations into metastable austenitic steels while suppressing the phase transformation.
The terrace-like phase boundaries in TMT samples serve as more effective dislocation sources.
